Before we begin

An apprenticeship or traineeship combines paid work with formal training. These statistics count training contracts, not unique people. “Trade” covers technicians and trades workers; “non-trade” covers other occupations. These nationally consistent groups are not exact synonyms for apprenticeships and traineeships.

01

THE NATIONAL PICTURE

After the surge, a smaller system.

Active contracts peaked in 2022 within this ten-year window. Both groups have since contracted, but non-trade training has fallen much faster.

02

THE GEOGRAPHY OF TRAINING

Size is only half the picture.

New South Wales has the most active contracts. Relative to the resident population, Tasmania has the greatest concentration. These two views answer different questions.

Maps: ABS ASGS 2021 state boundaries, simplified; Albers equal-area projection. Offshore detail is omitted. The ACT is labelled with a leader. Population: ABS, December 2025; numerator and denominator refer to the same date.

Population adjustment changes the comparison: Tasmania’s 7,375 contracts are a small national share, but its training intensity is about 1.6 times Victoria’s.

Population denominators include residents of all ages. Differences in age structure, industries and cross-border work can affect comparisons.

03

THE WORK BEHIND THE NUMBERS

Different occupations. Different trajectories.

Trade training is concentrated in a few large groups. Beyond the trades, some caring occupations have held up better than administrative and sales pathways.

04

PEOPLE & PATHWAYS

Participation is not the same as completion.

The system reaches different communities and supports different working arrangements. Annual starts and finishes tell us about activity, but they do not track the same people through training.

WHAT TO TAKE AWAY

A smaller system, with a changing mix.

The national decline hides important differences. Non-trade training has contracted more sharply, Tasmania has high training intensity despite its small total, and caring roles have gained prominence within leading non-trade occupations.

To understand someone’s chance of finishing, we would need cohort completion data. Dividing this year’s completions by this year’s commencements would mix people who started in different years.

SOURCES & METHODS

Where these numbers come from

Training contracts

NCVER (2026), Apprentices and trainees 2025: December quarter, released 22 June 2026. National Apprentice and Trainee Collection no. 127, March 2026 estimates; activity to 31 December 2025. Charts use published figure/table values, transcribed and checked.

Counts are rounded to the nearest five. Recent estimates may be revised for up to seven quarters. Totals may differ from sums of displayed groups because of rounding or unknown classifications.

Population & geography

ABS (2026), National, state and territory population, December 2025, released 18 June 2026. State populations are converted from published thousands to persons. Rates are active contracts ÷ resident population × 1,000.

ABS ASGS 2021 state boundaries, generalised and simplified for national-scale display. The eight state/territory records are joined by name; Other Territories are omitted from maps. The national population includes Other Territories.

Definitions, calculation choices & limitations
  • In-training is a stock at 31 December. It must not be added across quarters. Annual activity counts cover the full calendar year.
  • Trade means ANZSCO major group 3 (technicians and trades workers). Non-trade means other occupation groups. This is not a one-to-one apprenticeship/traineeship distinction.
  • Contract location and resident population describe different concepts; per-resident rates measure system intensity, not an individual’s enrolment probability.
  • The heatmap uses each occupation group’s 2021 count as its denominator. The rank chart compares a fixed set: the top ten non-trade occupations selected by 2025 count.
  • Waffle squares are rounded to whole percentage points; the adjacent percentage uses the published counts. Cohort categories overlap and should not be summed.
  • Mosaic widths use the sum of the two published trade classifications (282,425); the published national total is 282,430. Segment heights use NCVER’s rounded percentages, so rectangle areas are approximate shares.
  • Percentage calculations from rounded counts may differ slightly from NCVER’s percentages calculated from unrounded data. Published state changes are retained as given.
  • These descriptive comparisons do not establish the effect of policy, individual choices or employer behaviour.
